📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a Upcoming York City bill.
  • In a recent development, this weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a Upcoming York City bill.

In a recent development, this weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for Upcoming Yorkers.”.

Recent findings suggest that amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries.

Amazon previously sent mailers to NYC residents regarding a new headquarters (which was subsequently scrapped), but political messaging on packages is unprecedented for Amazon, which hasn’t used its delivery boxes to lobby for political causes before.

Sources indicate that last week, Amazon made another uncharacteristic move by showing NYC shoppers a homepage banner ad—which I see when logging in to Amazon as of this writing—and an in-app pop-up that also urges opposition to the bill. The banner and pop-up include a link to a blog where Amazon says the law would force it to consider moving operations outside of NYC and lead to “slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Fresh York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, however, support the bill.

By using its packages, website, and app to advocate against the bill, Amazon hopes to leverage its large customer base to push a political ideal. This raises concerns about whether it’s presenting the debate fairly, the appropriateness of using an e-commerce platform for political purposes, and whether we’ll see more political messaging while shopping with Amazon or other companies in the future.

As it stands, some shoppers are already put off by Amazon’s lobbying.

“Something about this just feels off to me,” a Reddit user who apparently received a package with the sticker wrote.

In a statement to CNBC last week, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel remarked the manufacturer is using the homepage and in-app messages to be “transparent with our customers” about what the proposed law “would cause them if it passes as written.”.

As of Friday, Amazon shoppers had sent over 60,000 emails to NYC Councilmembers opposing the bill, NBC Fresh York reported.

It has been revealed that the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection will decide whether to advance the bill to the entire council. The date for that vote hasn’t been set yet.

Google’s graphic for connecting Wallet, Drive and other apps to Personal Intelligence in Search.

Sources indicate that google is rolling out an opt-in connection between Google Wallet and Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode, with Drive and the Gemini app to follow in the coming weeks. The read-only Wallet link lets AI Mode suggest ways to cut spending and use card rewards.

In a recent development, google Search’s AI Mode can now use your Google Wallet to give more personal answers, the company revealed on Monday. Drive and the Gemini app will follow in the coming weeks. It is the latest step in Google’s AI overhaul of Search, unveiled at I/O in May.

The opt-in connections are part of Personal Intelligence, which already lets AI Mode draw on Gmail, Calendar and Photos. With Wallet linked, AI Mode can suggest ways to trim spending and make the most of cash-back and reward points on cards stored in Wallet. Google notes the link is read-only, so AI Mode cannot move, manage or invest money.

According to recent reports, with Drive connected, AI Mode can use documents, spreadsheets and PDFs, for example to draw up a blueprint for tax season. Linking the Gemini app will let ideas explored in one carry over to the other.

Google released the same Wallet link in Gemini for US users ten days ago, and OpenAI has let some ChatGPT users link bank accounts since May. Users can switch each app on or off under Connected Apps in Search Personalization, and a new icon will show what personal context a response used.

#2955. Charging to 100% Every Night Wears Down Your Phone’s Battery. Try This Instead

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1059 w)

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Charging to 100% Every Night Wears Down Your Phone’s Battery. Try This Instead

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple states iPhone batteries are most comfortable at temperatures between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit, and charging outside that range, whether in a hot car or inside a thick case, speeds up wear.
  • Recent findings suggest that voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss.
  • Age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple states iPhone batteries are most comfortable at temperatures between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit, and charging outside that range, whether in a hot car or inside a thick case, speeds up wear. Heat is one of two things that age a phone battery faster than normal use. The other is time spent at 100%. Avoiding both takes very little effort, and the charge limit settings on iPhones, Pixels and Galaxy phones handle part of the job for you. Here’s how to charge in a way that keeps your battery healthier for longer.

Recent findings suggest that voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss. The damage may not appear immediately, but it’s measurable after one year and obvious after two.

Age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably. Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity faster when they spend extended time at the top of their charge range, which is precisely where an overnight charge leaves them. The fix doesn’t require a new phone or even a new charger. It requires a small adjustment to a habit most people have never thought twice about.

Keeping a lithium-ion cell pinned at 100% creates voltage stress, and the heat generated from sitting on a charger could end up meaning the difference between keeping your current phone a little longer or having to buy a fresh one. So once and for all, does keeping your phone plugged in really hurt the battery? Here’s what the experts suggest.

It isn’t about immediate damage but rather how fast your battery ages over time. Understanding the difference between what will and won’t break your phone is key. Here is the truth about your charging habits.

Battery health is not just about how many times you charge your phone. It is also about how it manages voltage, temperature and maintenance. Lithium-ion batteries age fastest when they are exposed to extreme levels: 0% and 100%.

Recent findings suggest that keeping these batteries near full charge for long stretches of time puts additional voltage stress on the cathode and electrolyte. This is why many devices use “trickle charging” or temporarily pause at 100%, topping up only when needed.

Recent findings suggest that still, the biggest threat is not overcharging, but heat. When your phone is plugged in and running demanding apps, it produces heat that accelerates chemical wear inside the battery. If you are gaming, streaming or charging on a hot day, that extra warmth does far more harm than leaving the cable plugged in overnight.

According to recent reports, the Apple battery guide describes lithium-ion batteries as “consumable components” that naturally lose capacity over time. To slow that decline, iPhones use Optimized Battery Charging, which learns your daily routine and pauses charging at about 80% until just before you typically unplug, reducing time spent at high voltage.

Apple also advises keeping devices between 0 and 35 degrees Celsius (32 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit) and removing certain cases while charging to improve heat dissipation. You can read more on the official Apple battery support page.

According to recent reports, samsung offers a similar feature called Battery Protect, found in the One UI battery and device care settings. When enabled, it caps charging at 85%, which helps reduce stress during long charging sessions.

According to recent reports, other Android makers like Google, OnePlus and Xiaomi include comparable options — often called Adaptive Charging, Optimized Charging or Battery Care — that dynamically slow power delivery or limit charge based on your habits. These systems make it safe to leave your phone plugged in for extended periods without fear of overcharging.

Even with these safeguards, some conditions can accelerate battery wear. As mentioned before, the most common culprit is high temperatures. Even for a short period of time, leaving your phone charging in direct sunlight, in a car or under a pillow can push temperatures into unsafe zones.

Heavy use, such as gaming or 4K video editing, while charging can also cause temperature spikes which can degrade the battery faster. And cheap, uncertified cables or adapters may deliver unstable current that stresses cells. If your battery is already several years old, it will naturally be more sensitive to this kind of strain.

Recent findings suggest that there is no need to overhaul your habits, but a few tweaks can help your battery age gracefully. Start by turning on the optimization tools on your phone: Optimized Battery Charging on iPhones, Battery Protect on Samsung devices and Adaptive Charging on Google Pixels. These systems learn your routine and adjust charging speed so your phone is not sitting at 100% all night.

Keep your phone cool while charging. According to Apple, phone batteries perform best between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit (16 to 22 degrees Celsius). If your phone feels hot, remove its case or move it to a better ventilated or shaded spot. Avoid tossing your phone under a pillow or too close to other electronics, like your laptop. Skip wireless chargers that trap heat overnight. Use quality chargers and cables from your phone manufacturer or trusted brands. Those cheap “fast-charge” kits you find online often deliver inconsistent current, which can cause long-term complications.

Finally, try not to obsess over topping off the charge. It is perfectly fine to plug in your phone during the day for short bursts. Lithium-ion batteries actually prefer frequent, shallow charges rather than deep full cycles. There is no need to keep it between 20% and 80% all the time, but just avoid extremes when possible.

According to recent reports, keeping your phone plugged in overnight or on your desk all day will not destroy its battery. That is a leftover myth from a different era of tech. Modern phones are smart enough to protect themselves, and features such as Optimized Battery Charging or Battery Protect do most of the heavy lifting for you.

Still, no battery lasts forever. The best way to slow the inevitable is to manage heat, use quality chargers and let the software on your phone do its job. Think of it less as “babying” your battery and more as charging with intention. A few mindful habits today can keep your phone running strong for years to come.

From Amazfit and RingConn to Samsung, these alternatives offer different ways to avoid Oura's recurring fees.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Sources indicate that oura's Ring 5 starts at $399, but that's just the hardware. To get detailed sleep, recovery and health insights, you'll need to pay $5.99 per month or $69.99 a year for a membership. Without that subscription, you can only get three scores per day: Sleep, Activity and Readiness. With two years of membership, the base ring costs almost $539 before taxes, so it's a pretty expensive health tracker that can't even tell time.

Sources indicate that as we mentioned in our Oura Ring 5 review, there's still a lot to love about its slimmer design and weeklong battery life. However, some competitors monitor similar health data without the monthly fee, and others are much cheaper. We compared their current US prices, included features and independent reviews to see where those savings come with compromises.

The Amazfit Helio Ring is priced around $161, significantly lower than Oura's entry-level ring. It monitors sleep, heart rate and recovery via the Zepp app, which can also integrate data from an Amazfit smartwatch. Helio owners can at the moment get Zepp Aura Premium for free. There are some obvious compromises, though. The ring is only available in sizes 8, 10 and 12, and Amazfit rates battery life at up to four days. So while the price is tempting, it's only worth it if one of those sizes fits you.

Sources indicate that another budget-friendly choice is Renpho's LYNX, which is $179.99 on sale from $199.99. It comes with a portable charging case, is compatible with iOS and Android and can monitor sleep, stress and activity, without needing a subscription. Unfortunately, hands-on testing has shown that the heart-rate data were not consistent during exercise, and sleep data were questionable too. Its app also provided little analysis of the data it gathered, so the savings are harder to appreciate when you're second-guessing the readings.

It has been revealed that the RingConn Gen 2 Air is priced at $199 and is said to last up to 10 days on a single charge, with heart rate, skin temperature and sleep monitoring without any additional fees. It comes with a charging dock rather than a portable battery case, while sleep apnea pattern monitoring is reserved for pricier RingConn models. If you're only interested in tracking your sleep without an additional monthly charge, those may be acceptable compromises.

In a recent development, samsung's Galaxy Ring, which we found somewhat basic and a bit pricey in our Galaxy Ring review, has a list price of $399.99, though Amazon has it presently listed for $324.99. The savings are down the road though, as Samsung doesn't charge a membership fee for its health-tracking features. It also comes with a charging case, as mentioned in our roundup of fitness trackers with no subscription fees. The issue is that it's Android-only and some Galaxy AI features require a compatible Samsung Galaxy phone, so iPhone consumers can cross this one off their lists.

Industry observers note that the Circular Ring 2 is priced at $349 and includes single-lead ECG readings, heart-rhythm monitoring and sleep tracking without requiring a subscription, though some advanced features demand an additional fee. Despite the impressive hardware, the software does leave a lot to be desired. Reviewers have found the app cluttered and slow to sync, though Circular has since released updates addressing connectivity issues. The firm also cautions that its health measurements aren't intended for medical diagnosis.

Lastly, the Ultrahuman Ring Pro is more expensive than Oura at $479. It comes with a charging case and free core health tracking, but some optional PowerPlugs cost extra. In our Ring Pro review, we noted that the detailed app and the battery life of about 10 days were good, but automatic workout detection sometimes failed to capture workouts. There's also legal uncertainty: Oura sued Ultrahuman again in October 2026, seeking to block US sales of the Ring Pro. An earlier patent ruling had already blocked imports of the Ring Air.

Recent findings suggest that the best stocking stuffers should surprise and delight, but too often, we miss the mark. Think: tacky socks, bulk chocolate candy from the clearance aisle, and ChapStick. Most of these last-minute gift ideas are just begging to be tossed in a junk drawer or the donation pile, never to see the light of day again. Granted, it's a fate they probably deserve.

It has been revealed that but that's a shame, because unpacking your stocking should be the perfect start to the happiest day of the year. So, we consulted our deep bench of shopping reporters, deal hunters, and product reviewers to find out what stocking stuffers they want to wake up to on Christmas morning.

In a recent development, we've gathered our favorite tiny-but-impressive gift ideas that can work for everyone on your holiday shopping list. So, whether you're searching for stocking stuffer ideas under $25 or something fancier that will catch them by surprise, we have more than 60 unique gifts to inspire you.
